title: What makes a good jazz musician; embouchure
summary: Howard's views on feel versus reading, his lip placement, and others' unusual embouchures.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: What makes a good jazz musician anyhow? I could figure that out.

Well it's just about the way I can figure it would make him good. It's something that he wants to do, and he just let go with it. Well do you think the reading helps? Well I don't, I wouldn't know exactly, but the reading would help him to play. They got some fellas to read, and that's but all, they don't have nothing with it. You know what I mean? But to my idea, the guy playing something, the way he feels he should play it, it should come out better.
Do you have any special tricks, you know, to make you play jazz better? Any kind of special way of playing your instrument?
No, I don't know, special way that I have noticed to make me, other than when I used to drink, well, some time I didn't feel like playing and get a taste, so well, that would change things.
Do you lip your horn in a special way?
Well, no, I put the pressure most on the top lip, right here.
I just wondered, I noticed some guy seemed to sort of turn their lip out.
And you just lip it regularly.
I put it regularly there, right at the center, here and there. I'm trying to remember who used to do that.
It might have been Kit Clayton or something.
Yeah, Clayton would play most with the mouthpiece down in the bottom lip.
Inside the bottom lip? Yeah. That's a funny way of playing. I know that I understand. Well it is.
I mean, Pop used to blow on the side, well on the side. Yeah, Celestine.
Yeah. Remember that, he looked funny. His mouth was all screwed around and everything.
He tells you, I mean the book tells you the proper way to play it, but then if you can't get it in any way it's comfortable to you, that's the way it goes.
